exam: A 3‑year‑old boy presents with recurrent skin abscesses. What is the first test you would order? — NBT test to assess neutrophil oxidative burst.
You find a negative NBT result. Which organism is most likely responsible for his current infection? — Staphylococcus aureus or Serratia marcescens.
A child with suspected CGD is started on prophylactic itraconazole. Why is this drug chosen? — It prevents Aspergillus infection, a common cause of mortality in CGD.
You have a patient with neutropenia and a negative NBT. What is the next step? — Perform DHR flow cytometry to confirm CGD or consider other causes of neutropenia.
A child with CGD develops a lung cavity. What imaging study is most useful? — Chest X‑ray followed by CT if available.
You are in a low‑resource setting and cannot perform DHR. What alternative confirms CGD? — Repeat NBT with careful technique or use a nitroblue tetrazolium reduction assay with a different dye.
ai.title: Nitroblue Tetrazolium Test
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: The NBT test evaluates neutrophil oxidative burst, helping diagnose chronic granulomatous disease and other phagocytic defects. It is a simple colour change assay used where advanced flow cytometry is unavailable.

b: Colourless NBT → blue formazan in normal neutrophils
sections.p: The NBT test measures the ability of neutrophils to reduce the colourless dye nitroblue tetrazolium to a blue formazan precipitate during a respiratory burst. A negative or weak reaction suggests a phagocytic defect.
Severity is graded by the proportion of neutrophils that reduce NBT: >80% normal, 50–80% mild defect, <50% severe defect. Clinical severity correlates with infection frequency.

The most common cause in low‑resource settings is chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). Other causes include severe combined immunodeficiency, neutropenia, and exposure to herbal toxins that inhibit NADPH oxidase.

b: Recurrent Staph aureus, Serratia marcescens, Aspergillus
sections.p: Patients present with recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, especially with catalase‑positive organisms. Skin abscesses, lymphadenitis, and granulomatous lesions are common.
The NBT test is the first line. If unavailable, a dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry assay is preferred. Blood cultures, chest X‑ray, and fungal imaging are adjuncts.
Severe infections, rapidly progressive abscesses, or failure to respond to antibiotics should prompt urgent evaluation for phagocytic defects.

b: Bone marrow transplant for definitive cure
sections.p: Treat the underlying infection aggressively with appropriate antibiotics or antifungals. Provide prophylaxis with trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole and itraconazole. Consider bone marrow transplant in confirmed CGD.
Regular monitoring for infections, immunizations (including pneumococcal and influenza), and early treatment of any new infection are essential.

b: SCID – normal NBT but low neutrophil count
sections.p: Other causes of neutropenia such as severe combined immunodeficiency or drug‑induced neutropenia may mimic CGD clinically but have different NBT results.
A false‑negative NBT can occur if the test is performed after antibiotic therapy or if neutrophils are immature. A false‑positive may arise from technical errors or contamination.

whenToSeekHelp: Failure to respond to standard antibiotics
